title: What Should I Discuss at My One-on-Ones
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This practical article lays out a specific structure for effective weekly one-on-ones, starting from the principle that the direct report's agenda, not the leader's, should drive the meeting. The author proposes a concrete 10-10-10 format — ten minutes for the report's topics, ten for leader feedback, ten for priorities and planning — and flags a commonly neglected agenda item: discussing talent below the direct report on a weekly cadence rather than waiting for formal talent reviews. The piece closes by naming one-on-ones as foundational to alignment, accountability, and relationships, deserving of a leader's highest priority.
points: Effective weekly one-on-ones should be driven by the direct report's agenda first, not the leader's, to create genuine two-way dialogue.
The recommended structure is a 10-10-10 format: 10 minutes for the report's agenda, 10 for leader feedback, 10 for priorities and planning.
A frequently overlooked one-on-one topic is talent below the direct report — leaders should track this weekly rather than saving it for formal talent reviews.
Reviewing recent 'wins' as part of the conversation makes one-on-ones more motivational, not just administrative.
quotes: Best practice suggests that one-on-one meetings between a leader and a team member should occur weekly and be driven by the report, not the leader.

By insisting that team members drive the meeting, the discussion is more likely to become a two-way dialogue, as opposed to the one-way monologues leaders too often create when they control the meeting from the outset.
The ideal structure for a weekly one-on-one is the 10-10-10 format: 10 minutes for the direct report to share what they want to discuss, 10 minutes for the leader to provide feedback

One topic often overlooked is a discussion of talent below the direct report. Discussing who is on track or off track and what talent issues should be on the leader’s radar shouldn’t wait for talent reviews.
One-on-ones are the building blocks of alignment, accountability, and relationships. Good leaders make them the highest priority.
